prime.problem: To say whether an operation is slow because of math or because of data movement, you need more than a FLOP count. A FLOP-only estimate says a batch-1 matmul on an H100 takes 0.03 µs; it really takes about 10 µs because of the bytes. Every is it memory-bound? answer in the chapter rests on the roofline.
prime.fits: Third card. perf-1's roofline intuition gave you the picture; this card gives the book's algebra (T<sub>math</sub>, T<sub>comms</sub>, the lower and upper bounds, arithmetic intensity) that the next three cards apply to linear layers, attention and the whole step.
expect: network rooflines, where the threshold moves to D
prime.goal: Compute an operation's intensity, compare it with a chip's ridge, bracket its run time, and explain why a matmul's intensity grows with batch while a dot product's never does.

attend: Why is max(T<sub>math</sub>, T<sub>comms</sub>) a lower bound and their sum an upper bound, and what physical assumption separates them?
What does dividing both sides of T<sub>math</sub> > T<sub>comms</sub> by bytes buy you?
Why does a dot product's intensity approach ½ however long the vectors get, while a matmul's grows with B?
Why doesn't sharding one matmul across more chips move its critical batch, and what does move it?
When two chips split a matmul along D and swap partial sums, why does B cancel and D become the threshold?

must: Every op needs time for its math (FLOPs ÷ peak) and for its bytes (bytes ÷ bandwidth) → with perfect overlap it takes the max, with none the sum → one comparison, intensity(op) vs peak ÷ bandwidth, says which bound applies

A matmul X[B,D]·Y[D,F] loads the weights DF once however many rows B pass through → FLOPs grow with B, bytes barely do → intensity ≈ B when B ≪ D, F → above ≈ 240 (v5e) or 295 (H100) it turns compute-bound
A dot product does ~2N FLOPs on ~4N bytes with nothing reused → intensity is stuck near ½ at any N → no amount of size makes it compute-bound on these chips

Across chips the bandwidth is the link, not HBM → splitting a matmul along D makes both FLOPs and bytes sent grow with B → B cancels, and the threshold becomes D > 2 × C/W<sub>ici</sub> (8,755 on v5e ICI)
elevated: The B > 240 rule is the B ≪ D, F approximation → at D = F = 4096 the exact crossover is ≈ 272 on v5e and ≈ 345 on H100 → small matrices need a bigger batch than the headline number
NVIDIA headline tensor FLOPs assume 2:4 sparsity → dense bf16 is half (9.89e14) → using the sparse number would double the H100 ridge by mistake
reference: the hardware-intensity table (v5e int8 480, ICI 4,378, H100 fp8 591, H200 206)
the Q3 FLOP/s-vs-B table from the book's plotting code
80–85% achievable peak on GPUs vs ~95% on TPUs

compress.prompt: Without looking, write the two time formulas, the two bounds and the one inequality that decides the regime. Then sketch the roofline plot (log intensity on x, achievable FLOP/s on y), mark the ridge for H100, and place a dot product and a B = 1,024 matmul on it.
checklist: T<sub>math</sub> = FLOPs / peak; T<sub>comms</sub> = bytes / bandwidth
max is the lower bound (full overlap), sum the upper bound (none), at most 2× apart
compute-bound iff FLOPs/byte > peak/bandwidth (240 v5e, 295 H100)
matmul intensity ≈ B because weights load once; dot product ≈ ½

retrieve.q: Explain in terms of reuse why batching raises a matmul's intensity but can't raise a dot product's.
answer: in a matmul every weight byte is used by all B rows, so FLOPs scale with B while the weight bytes don't
in a dot product every byte is used exactly once; there is nothing shared to amortise
intensity rises only when loaded bytes are reused by more work

retrieve.q: Walk through the B = 1,024, D = F = 4096 matmul on v5e: FLOPs, bytes, both times, both bounds, and the verdict.
You can buy either twice the bandwidth or twice the peak FLOPs. For a batch-1 decode matmul and for a B = 1,024 prefill matmul, which purchase helps, and why?
answer: batch-1 decode is far left of the ridge (intensity ≈ 1): only bandwidth helps; more FLOPs just idle
B = 1,024 is right of the ridge: only more FLOPs help
more bandwidth also lowers the ridge (H100 295 → H200 206), so more ops become compute-bound

retrieve.q: In the book's Q4 every batch element has its own weight matrix. What happens to intensity as B grows, and what real serving situation has the same shape?
answer: bytes become BD + BDF + BF, so the weight bytes grow with B too
intensity stays ≈ 2 whatever B is: always comms-bound
decode attention has this shape: each sequence reads its own KV cache, so batching adds bytes as fast as FLOPs

compare.q: perf-1 introduced the roofline as a picture. What does this card's max/sum bracket and exact-bytes crossover let you do that the picture alone couldn't?
answer: predict a time, not just a regime: the true time lies between max and sum
find the exact crossover including the BD and BF terms (≈ 345 on H100 at D = F = 4096, not 295)
apply the same algebra to chip-to-chip links (network rooflines), where the threshold moves to D

compare.q: Matmul intensity ≈ B; decode attention intensity ≈ 1. Using this card's language, what is the one design fact that makes the difference?
answer: a linear layer's weights are shared across the batch, so more rows reuse the same bytes
attention's weights are each sequence's own KV cache, so more sequences add their own bytes
reuse per loaded byte, not model size, sets intensity

predict.q: Take a bigger square matmul, D = F = 8,192, on an H100. Commit first: is the exact crossover batch above or below 295, and by roughly how much compared with the D = F = 4096 case (≈ 345)?
predict.answer: Above 295, but closer to it: solving BDF / (BD + DF + BF) = 295 gives B ≈ 318, versus ≈ 345 at 4096. Bigger matrices make the BD and BF terms relatively smaller, so the exact value approaches the B ≪ D, F approximation of 295 from above.

apply.task: Extend labs/roofline.py (or do it by hand) for an H100 bf16 matmul with D = F = 8,192 at B = 64: compute FLOPs, exact bytes, intensity, Tmath, Tcomms and the bound. Then solve for the exact crossover batch. Finally, name one change to the op that would make B = 64 compute-bound without changing the chip.
apply.done: You get intensity ≈ 63.0, T<sub>math</sub> ≈ 8.7 µs vs T<sub>comms</sub> ≈ 40.7 µs (memory-bound) and a crossover of ≈ 318, and your change raises reuse per byte (for example, int8 weights with bf16 math halves the batch needed).
